extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (schools, colleges, universities), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, counsel implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance explaining permissible evidentiary standards (preponderance or clear and convincing), how recipients must select and apply a single standard consistently in Title IX sexual harassment formal complaints, and related procedural constraints and protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of actionable sexual harassment under §106.30
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct constituting actionable harassment under §106.30 must be either serious misconduct constituting quid pro quo harassment or Clery Act/VAWA sex offenses, or meet the Davis standard of being severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive denying a person equal educational access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explicitly ties §106.30 actionable harassment to quid pro quo, Clery/VAWA sex offenses, or the Davis severe/pervasive/objectively offensive framework; this defines the scope of Title IX sexual harassment for which the grievance procedures and evidentiary rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on treating restriction of First Amendment rights as evidence of no deliberate indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations explicitly prohibit the Department from deeming recipients' restriction of rights protected under the First Amendment to be evidence that the recipient was not deliberately indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients' restriction of speech/First Amendment activity cannot be used by the Department as evidence that the recipient responded appropriately (i.e., was not deliberately indifferent) to allegations of sexual harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted evidentiary standards (recipient choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must select between the preponderance of the evidence standard and the clear and convincing evidence standard, and may apply either standard to reach determinations in Title IX formal complaints alleging sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department permits either standard because the robust procedural protections in §106.45 mean either may produce fair, reliable outcomes; the Department does not require a criminal 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard and is not promoting one evidentiary standard over the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to apply the chosen standard consistently to all formal complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must apply the selected evidentiary standard consistently to all formal complaints alleging Title IX sexual harassment regardless of whether the respondent is a student or an employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(1)(vii) and §106.45(b)(7)(i) require that the same standard be the operative 'degree of confidence' decision‑makers must have across all formal Title IX sexual harassment cases so complainants face a predictable grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same evidentiary standard for student and faculty/employee cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations require that the same standard of evidence be used in student-respondent cases and in employee/faculty-respondent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement aims to promote fairness, predictability, and consistency across complainants; the Department acknowledges CBAs and State laws may constrain recipients and discusses renegotiation or selecting the alternate standard as potential solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' selection not tied to non-Title IX proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department removed the NPRM language that would have required use of the preponderance standard in Title IX cases only if the recipient used that standard for non-sexual misconduct with similar sanctions; recipients' selection of standard for Title IX cases is not restricted by non-Title IX standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are free to choose either standard for Title IX cases without regard to what standard they use in other disciplinary contexts; the Department declined to inspect or regulate how recipients handle non-Title IX misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to use criminal standard ('beyond a reasonable doubt')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has never required application of the criminal 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard in Title IX proceedings; the Department will not require that standard as it is unnecessary for due process or fairness in noncriminal Title IX grievance processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department is not aware of any appellate decision requiring the criminal standard in Title IX matters and believes robust §106.45 protections allow civil standards (preponderance or clear and convincing) to achieve fair outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective, unbiased assessment of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Under either chosen standard, the recipient is obligated to assess credibility based on objective evaluation of the evidence and not due to the party's status as complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must avoid bias for or against complainants or respondents or based on respondent status (student/employee/faculty); credibility determinations should be grounded in objective evidence evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant notice and predictability about the standard of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainants should know which standard of evidence their school, college, or university has selected and that it will apply regardless of the identity, status, or position of authority of the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing predictability helps complainants understand the 'degree of confidence' decision‑makers must have; the selected standard should be applied uniformly so complainants face the same process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' flexibility and autonomy to choose appropriate standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department permits recipients to select the standard that best meets the recipient's unique needs and reflects its values, recognizing recipients are in the best position to decide what level of confidence decision-makers should require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the Department permits choice, it also acknowledges external constraints (CBAs, State law) and suggests possible remedies (e.g., renegotiating CBAs); the Department does not intend to coerce selection of either standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding disparate treatment of complainants based on respondent status or bargaining power
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must not adjudicate a student-complainant's formal complaint differently based on whether the alleged harasser is a student or an employee; the grievance process should not vary based on identity/status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is intended to prevent exacerbating power differentials (e.g., faculty leverage) by imposing a higher evidentiary burden on complainants who allege harassment by employees than for those alleging harassment by students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on fair, reliable, and predictable outcomes in Title IX grievance processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's approach emphasizes that either evidentiary standard may be applied to reach fair, accurate, and reliable determinations regarding responsibility in Title IX grievance processes, given the procedural protections afforded by §106.45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations aim to ensure complainants' equal educational access through reliable resolution processes, while balancing concerns about potential reputational or employment consequences for respondents.
